subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Saurabh, you're doing that thing I used to do. Nodding when you don't understand. I can see it from here.
Let me tell you something. When I was a girl of twenty-four, new in the accounts department of the old textile mill, I heard the word 'reconciliation' fifty times in my first week. I had no idea what it meant. I wrote it on my palm to look up at home. I was sure if I asked, they'd send me back.
One afternoon Mr Kulkarni handed me a file and said, 'Sonali, reconcile this.' I stood there. Then I said, 'Sir, I'm sorry. What does reconcile mean here, exactly?'
He didn't laugh. He pulled up a chair, showed me two ledgers, and said, 'You match these, line by line. That's all.' Then he went back to his tea.
That's all, Saurabh. Nobody laughed. So, what is it you want to ask?

qa.q: Where did Sonali write the word 'reconciliation' to look it up at home?
qa.a: She wrote it on her palm.

qa.q: What was Sonali afraid would happen if she asked Mr Kulkarni?
qa.a: She was afraid of being humiliated and even of being sent back for not knowing.

qa.q: What is Sonali encouraging Saurabh to do?
qa.a: She is inviting Saurabh to ask the question openly, since asking basic things is normal and usually gets a plain, kind answer.

qa.q: How might Saurabh feel hearing that Mr Kulkarni didn't laugh?
qa.a: Saurabh may feel relief and less fear about asking, seeing that the humiliation Saurabh dreads may never come.

grounding: It shows a young employee asking a basic question, getting a kind, matter-of-fact reply, and the fear of hiding ignorance starting to loosen.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job

The front page closed at 11:20, and it was 11:02 when the night editor dropped a story on Nikita's desk. 'Needs a kicker. Quick.'
Nikita, three weeks at the newspaper, had heard 'kicker' a dozen times. She had nodded every time.
She searched her notes. Nothing. The clock over the news desk ticked. She thought of guessing, of writing anything and hoping.
Gautam, the chief sub-editor, was at the next desk, headphones on, fixing a headline. Her heart was banging.
She tapped his shoulder. 'Sorry, basic question. What exactly is a kicker?'
He slid one headphone off. 'The small line above the headline. Two or three words. Sets the tone. Like "Monsoon woes".' He put the headphone back.
That was it. No sigh. No look.
Nikita wrote the kicker in two minutes. At 11:18 she sent the page. Her hands had stopped shaking.

qa.q: What time did the front page close?
qa.a: The front page closed at 11:20.

qa.q: What was Nikita afraid of before she tapped Gautam's shoulder?
qa.a: She was afraid of looking foolish for not knowing a word she had heard a dozen times and nodded at.

qa.q: What did Nikita's choice to ask show her about asking basic questions?
qa.a: It showed that a quick, honest question gets a plain answer and saves time, while hiding would have meant guessing under deadline.

qa.q: How does Gautam seem to see Nikita's question?
qa.a: He treats it as an ordinary work question, answering briefly and going back to his headline without judgement.

grounding: It shows a new journalist under deadline asking a basic question and getting a kind, matter-of-fact reply, so the fear of exposing ignorance loosens.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
I'd been at the publishing house five weeks, nodding every time someone said "print run" or "proof pass", when the proofs of my first book came back with a note: Check the imprint page. I had no idea what an imprint page was.
I spent an hour searching old files, too scared to ask. Finally, ears burning, I walked to Tarun's desk. He's been in production for eight years. "This is probably a stupid question," I said, "but what exactly is the imprint page?"
He didn't laugh. He didn't sigh. He pulled a book off his shelf, flipped to the back of the title page and said, "This one. Copyright line, edition, printer. Takes five minutes. Want me to check yours after?"
That was it. No humiliation. I walked back feeling oddly light. Later I asked him two more things, and each time it felt less like confessing. I'm Amandeep, and I'm starting to think not knowing isn't a crime here.

qa.q: How long has Tarun been in production?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel walking to Tarun's desk?
qa.a: Amandeep felt scared and embarrassed, ears burning, expecting to be judged for a basic question.

qa.q: What could Amandeep do next to keep this going?
qa.a: Keep asking small questions early, like the two later ones, rather than searching alone for an hour.

qa.q: How might Tarun have seen the question?
qa.a: Tarun likely saw it as an ordinary newcomer's question and was happy to help, without judging at all.

grounding: A newcomer finally asks a basic question, gets a kind, matter-of-fact reply, and the belief that ignorance must be hidden starts to loosen.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job

Team lead's note, Wednesday stand-up
Something small but worth recording. Akash, three weeks in, has been silent in every stand-up and staying late most nights. Today, when Jaya mentioned the staging server, Akash half raised a hand and said, "Sorry, this is basic, but what's the difference between staging and production here?" His voice shook a little.
Jaya answered plainly: "Staging is where we test; production is what customers see. Good question, actually. The names confuse everyone at first." Then she drew a quick box diagram on the whiteboard, and two others took photos of it.
I watched Akash's shoulders drop. At lunch he asked Jaya two more questions, and he left at six-thirty today, the first time since he joined.
Action for me: add a glossary page to our onboarding notes and ask Akash to help write it, since he has just found some of the gaps.

qa.q: What did Akash ask in the stand-up?
qa.a: What's the difference between staging and production here?

qa.q: What does Akash's shaking voice suggest about how he felt asking?
qa.a: He felt afraid and exposed, expecting the basic question to humiliate him.

qa.q: What did the team lead plan next, and why is it useful?
qa.a: The team lead planned a glossary for onboarding and asked Akash to help, turning his gaps into a resource for others.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt answering the question?
qa.a: Jaya likely found it ordinary and useful, since she said the names confuse everyone and others photographed her diagram.

grounding: A team lead's note shows a new hire asking a basic question, receiving a kind, plain answer, and his fear of exposure easing.

subtopic: Imposter feelings at a new job
passage:
Thursday, 11 p.m.
Did it. Finally asked.
For two weeks everyone on the news desk has been saying "check the slug", "change the slug", and I've been nodding like I knew. Tonight the chief sub said, "Saurabh, fix the slug on page four," and I froze at my screen.
So I leaned over to Chaitanya and whispered, "What's a slug? Sorry." My heart was going like a drum. I was sure Chaitanya would laugh, or tell the whole desk.
Chaitanya just said, "Oh, the short working name for the story, top left. Everyone asks that in week one," and went back to typing. That was all. Nobody looked up.
I fixed it in thirty seconds. I spent two weeks terrified of a thirty-second answer.
Tomorrow I'm going to ask what a "widow" means on the layout. I think.

qa.q: What did the chief sub ask Saurabh to fix?
qa.a: The slug on page four.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel just before whispering the question?
qa.a: Saurabh felt terrified and embarrassed, sure Chaitanya would laugh or tell the whole desk.

qa.q: What small step does Saurabh plan next, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Asking what a 'widow' means tomorrow; asking early and small stops confusion from building for weeks.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya have seen the whispered question?
qa.a: Chaitanya treated it as a normal week-one question, probably without noticing how nervous Saurabh was.

grounding: A new sub-editor asks a basic question, the reply is matter-of-fact, and the feared humiliation never comes.
